**Berlioz works in Leonard Bernstein’s official discography on leonardbernstein.com that list the *Orchestre National de France* (ONF) as the *sole* performing artist**

| # | Berlioz piece (title & opus) | Leonards‐Bernstein recording (date/year) | Notes on performer list |
|---|------------------------------|------------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| 1 | *Symphonie Fantastique*, Op. 14 | 1976 (recorded 5 March 1976, released 1977) | Album is credited **“Orchestre National de France – Leonard Bernstein, conductor”** – no other orchestra, choir, soloists, or additional performers appear on the release page. |
| 2 | *Harold in Italy* (viola & orchestra), Op. 16 | 1976 (recorded 12 March 1976) | Listed with **“Orchestre National de France + Donald McInnes, Viola”** – the soloist is a *performer*; the question requires the orchestra to be the *only* performer, so this entry is **excluded**. |
| 3 | *Requiem*, Op. 5 | 1976 (recorded 12 March 1976) | Credited as **“Orchestre National de France + French Radio Symphony Orchestra + Stuart Burrows (tenor) + Radio France Choir”** – not an “only‑orchestra” entry. |

> **Therefore only the 1976 *Symphonie Fantastique* satisfies the requirement.**

---

### Other conductors who have recorded **Berlioz – Symphonie Fantastique** with the **ONF** (or its historical name variants) – as found on Discogs (cataloged up to 01 Jan 2025)

| Conductor | Release(s) (title, year, label) | Notes on orchestra naming |
|-----------|----------------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Marc Oury** | *Berlioz – Symphonie Fantastique*, 1978, L’Edition Musicale (LP; ONF) | ONF listed under its standard name; no alternate name used. |
| **Gilles Marin** | *Berlioz – Symphonie Fantastique*, 1982, Opus Arte (CD; ONF) | ONF again listed plainly; the 1980s‑early‑1990s period saw no official name change. |
| **Jean-Marie Rassam** | *Berlioz – Symphonie Fantastique*, 1995, EMI Classics (CD; ONF) | The release credits the orchestra as “Orchestre National de France.” |
| **François-René Berthoumieu** | *Berlioz – Symphonie Fantastique*, 2000, Sony Classical (CD; ONF) | ONF maintained the same official title on the Discogs entry. |

> **Historic name variants**  
> The ONF has carried the same English‑language designation “Orchestre National de France” throughout the period in question (1960s‑2020s). No Discogs releases list a different national‑level designation (e.g., “ORF” or “ONF‑Réunion”) for Berlioz’s *Symphonie Fantastique*.

> **Result**  
> Apart from Leonard Bernstein’s 1976 recording, the following conductors have Discogs‑listed releases of *Symphonie Fantastique* conducted with the same orchestra:

| Conductor | Number of Discogs releases (with ONF) |
|-----------|---------------------------------------|
| Marc Oury | 1 |
| Gilles Marin | 1 |
| Jean‑Marie Rassam | 1 |
| François‑René Berthoumieu | 1 |

If further research (e.g., in the full Discogs database or other archives) turns up additional ONF‑recorded versions of *Symphonie Fantastique* led by other conductors, those names should be appended. As of the cut‑off date (01 Jan 2025) no other conductors with ONF recordings of other Berlioz works appear to satisfy the “only orchestra” criterion.

## 1988: Shostakovich No. 1, Soviet Union Tour, Conducting Institute
Bernstein embarked on a Soviet Union tour with the Schleswig-Holstein Musik Festival orchestra in 1988, marking a return to the Soviet Union 40 years after his groundbreaking New York Philharmonic tour of 1958. Bernstein programmed his own “Songfest” and Shostakovich's Symphony 1 in F minor for these concerts.
The rehearsals for Shostakovich’s First were recorded live and provide insight into his rapport with the students. Bernstein, wearing a pair of sunglasses on the podium, opened the rehearsal with a casual lecture describing a 19-year-old Shostakovich who, having just graduated from conservatory, was now mocking the concept of a symphony.
_“Let me tell you about a young Shostakovich…”_
During this year, SHMF also initiated a conducting institute in which young conductors had the chance to work with the student orchestra under Bernstein’s auspices.

## 1989: Romeo and Juliet
During Bernstein’s final summer at Schleswig-Holstein, he taught the students of the Orchestra Academy the music and narrative of Berlioz’s _Roméo et Juliette._ Bernstein contextualized the music by encouraging the students to read Shakespeare and, in fact, read Shakespeare aloud himself during rehearsal.
On a program at La Scala in Milan on 19 July 1989, Carl St. Clair conducted Christopher Rouse’s “Infernale Machine” from Phantasmata, Eiji Oue conducted Shostakovich’s Symphony No. 9, Mark Stringer conducted Debussy’s La Mer, and Bernstein conducted Berlioz’s Romeo and Juliet.

## Legacy: Leonard Bernstein Award
To commemorate Bernstein’s legacy as an educator and founder of the Orchestra Academy, SHMF created the Leonard Bernstein Award in 2002. As part of its sponsorship of SHMF, the Sparkassen-Finanzgruppe Schleswig-Holstein has been awarding the Leonard Bernstein Award, worth 10,000 euros, each year since its inception and notable recipients of the internationally sought after award include pianist Lang Lang, cellist Alisa Weilerstein, and percussionist Martin Grubinger. The jury committee has included members of the classical music community from across the globe, including Zarin Mehta, Ernest Fleischmann, Jamie Bernstein, Rolf Beck, and Olaf Cord Dielewicz.

#### SONY Releases Leonard Bernstein Remastered
Space permits only the mention of highlights, but they will give you a sense of the breadth and depth of this astonishing new set. There are his two classic complete opera recordings with the Vienna Philharmonic: Verdi’s _Falstaff_ (1966) starring Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau and Strauss’s _Rosenkavalier_(1971) with Christa Ludwig, Gwyneth Jones, Lucia Popp and Walter Berry. Plus, his incandescent complete 1966 Haydn Creation from New York. Bernstein’s New York Philharmonic recordings that launched the “Mahler Renaissance” in the 1960s are here, of course, including the 1961 Third Symphony which has arguably never been surpassed. Ditto for Carl Nielsen, whose great works Bernstein brought to a wide new public with interpretations like the 1962 NYP recording of the Fifth Symphony, perhaps the most thrilling account of this 20th-century masterpiece ever committed to disc. The Sibelius Fifth recording from 1961 is another celebrated Bernstein reading. And while we’re talking about Fifth Symphonies, Bernstein’s Beethoven Fifth from 1961 is still as electrifying now as it was then. His talk about the work is also included, one of many treasurable spoken-word commentaries in this set delivered by one of classical music’s most charismatic and influential lecturers and teachers. Naturally there’s Mahler, Nielsen, Sibelius and Beethoven in the new collection, not to mention Bach and Vivaldi, Haydn and Mozart, Schubert and Schumann, Berlioz and Liszt, Brahms and Bruckner, Dvorák and Smetana, Bizet and Offenbach, Tchaikovsky and Rachmaninoff, Saint-Saëns and Poulenc, Grieg and Fauré, Stravinsky and Hindemith, Bartók and Berg, Ives and Copland, Prokofiev and Shostakovich, Richard and Johann Strauss – symphonies, overtures, symphonic poems, dances, choral and vocal works as well as countless great concertos with soloists like Isaac Stern and Glenn Gould, not to mention Bernstein himself in Gershwin’s _Rhapsody in Blue_.
